## The server-resume test is three CTests (2026-10-13, branch test/server-resume-split, tests only, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** `server-resume` took 297.6 and 306.4 seconds on the hosted macOS runner, and its limit was raised to 600 as a stopgap (the record below); the CPU half is nearly all of its time on a runner without a device, so splitting the CPU and device halves shortens nothing.
- **What changed:** `llmx-server-resume-test` takes `cpu-resume` or `cpu-cache` beside `cpu` and `device`, and runs everything without an argument. The CPU half is two groups: the cases up to the files-lost-between-two-servers pair (`server-resume`, `cpu-resume`) and those from the disk tier's cap case on (`server-resume-cache`, `cpu-cache`), each with a limit of 300 seconds. The device half is `server-resume-device` with 300, which reports a skip and passes where there is no device. The cut is at the point that balances the two groups, found by timing every call of a whole run; the only edit in `tests/server_resume.cpp` is in `main()`, where the hybrid model is now built before the first group so both groups see it, and no case is removed, changed or reordered.
- **Shared state:** none between cases: each builds its own scheduler, model and directory (`DiskRoot` makes a directory of its own name and a random number), and the one global is the check counter. The weights, tokenizer and hybrid model `main()` builds are read-only.
- **Measured** (a Windows desktop, CPU build, one run each, the machine busy with nothing else; an earlier pair of runs overlapped other work and is not used): the old test, `cpu`, 225 s; a first cut at the end of the hybrid cases gave 59 s and 230 s and was moved; the cut that landed gives `cpu-resume` 116 s and `cpu-cache` 92 s, `device` 0 s. The hosted runs give each test's time on each runner.
- **Checks:** the old binary ran 50 case lines of results and the two new groups together the same 50 (compared by label, one line mangled by the interleaving of stdout and stderr in both). The count of checks printed is not fixed: the old test printed 832520 to 973196 over its runs, since cases that wait poll with a check in the loop, and the groups printed 73793 and 941243 (and 89246 and 961727 at the first cut), so the sum of the new counts cannot equal the old to the unit and was not asserted.
- **Gates:** CTest, the suite's `docs` and `dead-code` components and the hosted run; the macOS job of that run shows the three times.

## The server-resume test's limit is 600 seconds (2026-10-13, branch ci/server-resume-limit, the build file only, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** `server-resume` passed in 252.88 seconds of its 300 on the hosted macOS runner at 9758fbabb (run 38353196756), and was ended at 300 on the same runner on two heads of a branch under review within the hour (runs 38357998877 and 38362598549), every other test passing and no check of its own failing. The test has gained cases with each cache fix, and a landing could be cancelled by the runner it drew.
- **Done:** `TIMEOUT 600` for `server-resume` in `CMakeLists.txt`, the limit `server-passes-cpu` has. No case or check changes, and no wait in the test rides the limit: each fails by its own 60-second bound. Next, so the limit does not grow with the next cache fix: the CPU half is split by case group, the disk-tier and boundary cases apart from the resume cases, into two tests each under its own limit; splitting the CPU and device halves would shorten nothing on a runner without a device.
- **Gates:** CTest on the CPU on Linux at this head, the suite's `docs` and `dead-code` components, and the hosted run of this commit, whose macOS job shows the test under its new limit.

## A state read alone from disk keeps the host copy whose rows it is for (2026-10-13, branch fix/state-read-source, lands by fast-forward)

- **The defect, found by reading the restore path:** on a model that keeps a state, `Scheduler::prefetch` reads a state alone from disk where a history in memory holds its rows, and `start_read` then made room for that state by the rules of any read, which release host entries whose files are on disk first. With the host tier full of the one copy holding the rows, the room for the state was that copy's: the state arrived as a boundary with no rows, and the request read its prompt from the first token although the conversation was whole on disk.
- **Fix:** the read names the host entry its rows are in (`DiskRead::source`, from `rows_held`), and `release_written` and `drop_oldest_host` pass that entry over while the read's room is made and while it runs (`read_source`); `finish_read` makes it the newest entry again. Where the tier has no room for the state beside it, `start_read` reads the path's blocks with their state instead, a history of its own, for which the entry's room may go since its files hold it.
- **Not pinned, and why:** a device donor holding the rows, which no host room takes; and the time between the read's end and the request's admission in the same round, where the entry is the newest and a boundary left without rows is passed over by admission, the request reading its prompt.
- **Test:** `server-resume`, the hybrid model on one CPU, a pool of 1024 tokens and a disk tier written while idle. A 720-token conversation with a boundary at 256 is written, and another conversation's request moves its donor, 640 rows and a state, into a host tier of exactly that copy's size, the boundary making room. A request agreeing with it for 384 tokens must reuse 256 with one read from disk and one host copy used, its reply a fresh model's. The failing commit: "reused 0 tokens, 1 read from disk, 0 boundaries and 0 host copies used, 0 reads refused; before the request 1 host copies and 0 boundaries, against 256 reused from the 256 tokens read whole from disk".
- **The control arm, and what it does not show:** with room for the state beside the copy the boundary never leaves memory and serves over the copy's rows, 256 reused with nothing read, so it holds the expected outcome and not a state read alone beside its pinned source. States read alone with a source in host memory occur in the cases that were there before (four in a run of `server-resume`'s CPU half), which pass unchanged.
- **No failing-first arm for the protection while a read runs:** the pass-over of a read's source by other room-making during the read (`read_source` over the reads in flight) is reached by those older cases and fails nowhere without it; a case would need room taken by a second read or a copy leaving the devices while the first read runs.
- **Checked, Windows, MSVC, on the CPU:** the build, CTest, the suite's `docs` and `dead-code`. The tier's gates are run on the test machine at the head that lands.

## A boundary is chosen among those whose rows are held (2026-10-13, branch fix/boundary-candidates, lands by fast-forward)

- **The defect, found by reading the admission after the two fixes below:** `Scheduler::best_bound` gave the boundary sharing the most whole blocks with a request, whether or not any history in memory held its rows. A boundary is a state alone, so `enter` then looked for a donor or a host donor holding those rows, and finding none fell back to the donors, never trying a shorter boundary whose rows were held. `prefetch` made the same choice and then asked `rows_held` about that one boundary.
- **What it cost:** on a model that keeps a state a donor forks only at its own kept state, so a donor that holds a shorter boundary's rows is of no use without that boundary; the request read its history from the first token while a state and its rows were both in memory.
- **Fix:** `best_bound` passes over a boundary whose rows no donor and no host donor holds (`holds`), so it gives the longest boundary the request can use. It is the one choice for `enter` and `prefetch`; `prefetch` no longer asks `rows_held` after it.
- **Unchanged:** what `enter` does with the boundary chosen (the donor holding its rows, a host donor promoted first, the checkpoint slot, the pin while room is made) and its fallback to the donors where the promotion or the slot is not to be had; that fallback still does not try the next boundary down. The one case a loop there would add: the chosen boundary's rows in host memory alone, their promotion failing for device room, and a shorter boundary's rows in a device donor; the request then forks the best donor as before, a loss of reuse and not a wrong result.
- **Test:** `server-resume`, the hybrid model on one CPU, three requests at once and a host tier of 1 GiB. Two conversations share their first 300 tokens: the first, 420 tokens, leaves a boundary at 256 and a donor whose state is at 384; the second, 684 tokens, leaves a boundary at 512, and a job of other ids for its request supersedes its donor, which the next donor made replaces with no host copy. A request of 620 tokens continuing the second for 520 must reuse 256 through one boundary, its reply a fresh model's. The failing commit: "reused 0 tokens with 0 boundaries forked, 3 donors and 3 boundaries held before, against 256 from one boundary".
- **Not reached by the case:** `prefetch`'s line, which needs a disk tier the case does not make. There a boundary without rows now gives `best_bound` no candidate where `rows_held` gave false before, the same decision, and the three arms of the record below (a history larger than the host tier behind its boundary) hold it unchanged.
- **Checked, Windows, MSVC, on the CPU:** the build, CTest, the suite's `docs` and `dead-code`. The tier's gates are run on the test machine at the head that lands.

## The suite holds drafts kept, with a drafter that is right by construction (2026-10-13, branch test/kept-drafts-fixture, tests only, on test/argmax-slices-fixture, lands by fast-forward)

- **The gap:** no model fixture of the suite ever had a model drafter's draft kept. The MTP fixtures' weights are a fixed pseudo-random sequence, so their blocks predict nothing: 0 kept of 7 to 206 drafts fed in every run, greedy and seeded. A verify that wrongly refused every draft would change no output and no check through the CLI or on a device would see it; `spec` and `server-spec` hold kept drafts only with oracle proposers inside the inference layer.
- **Added:** the suite's `qwen35` component runs the Hv = 3 Hk model as its own draft model (`--drafter` naming the same file, a 1024-token context). Its greedy drafts are the model's greedy picks, so at temperature 0 every draft fed must be kept, at 1, 4, 8 and 16 drafts over 60 tokens (29 of 29 at one draft; 12, 12, 12 and 11 by position at four), with most of the tokens fed as drafts; greedy and seeded the output is that of drafts off. It runs the hybrid's mark and rerun and the draft model's own kept state, on the CPU and on the configured device.
- **Seeded, held to output only, with the reason:** at temperature 0.8 the same drafter keeps 0 of 13 at every position on this fixture, the model's distribution being nearly flat, so a greedy draft is seldom the draw; a requirement there would fail for no defect.
- **That it catches what it is for:** with `infer::accept` made to stop at every first row, the suite's `f32` draft checks pass and this case fails ("the model's own greedy drafts at --draft-max 1 were not all kept: 0 of 13").
- **Checked, Windows, MSVC:** the suite's `qwen35` on the CPU and with `--device vulkan:0` on a Radeon VII, with and without the planted fault on the CPU; `docs` and `dead-code`.

## The suite drafts through the argmax's slices (2026-10-13, branch test/argmax-slices-fixture, tests only, lands by fast-forward)

- **The gap it closes:** `argmax_rows` reduces a row past 4096 ids in slices (the record below), and every model fixture of the suite has a vocabulary under that, so on a device the embedded drafter ran the one-workgroup form everywhere but in `backend-vulkan`'s kernel cases and the gate's Qwen3.8-27B identity runs. The reviewer named a larger fixture as the follow-up.
- **Added:** the suite's `qwen35` component writes the MTP block's tiny fixture with a vocabulary of 8449 ids (`WIDE_VOCAB`, two slices and the fixtures' own 257 past them) and reads its drafts through `llmx-decode-probe` on the configured device and on the CPU: the pick and three drafts after each of three prompts must be the same ids and every draft row's logits within the F32 bound; the nine drafts must lie in more than the first slice, which they do (ids 234 to 6484). `generate --drafter embedded` is also held to `--drafter off` on it.
- **Why the probe and not the output:** a drafter's wrong id is a draft the verify refuses, so the output is the same bytes; the first form of this case compared output alone and a planted fault, the reduction returning the first slice's id, passed it. With the probe the same fault fails after the first prompt (the device drafts 3371 where the CPU drafts 6484). A vocabulary of one slice and 257 ids did not hold it either: all nine drafts lay in the first slice there, where that fault is right.
- **Not added, with the reason:** a requirement that a model drafter's verifies keep a draft. On every fixture of the suite that drafts with an MTP block the kept count is 0 (7, 22, 28 and up to 206 drafts fed, none kept, greedy and seeded), the weights being a fixed pseudo-random sequence that predicts nothing; only the qwen3 draft model keeps one, greedy. The requirement would fail on fixtures that are not at fault.
- **That it reaches the slices, shown and not assumed:** on a Radeon VII, `bench --model --drafter embedded --draft-max 1 --profile` counts 20 dispatches in a chain of one draft on the 257-id fixture and 21 on a fixture past 4096 ids, the second dispatch of the argmax. On the CPU, whose argmax has one form, it is one more model the drafter runs on.
- **Checked, Windows, MSVC:** the suite's `qwen35` with its tools required, on the CPU and with `--device vulkan:0` on the Radeon VII, the latter also with the fault planted, which fails it; `docs` and `dead-code`.

## A draft row's argmax reduces a row in slices (2026-10-12, branch perf/argmax-rows, lands by fast-forward)

- **Found by the draft's phase profile** (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, one MI50 and a tensor group of two, `bench --model --drafter embedded --profile`): `argmax_rows` took 1.18 and 1.14 ms of a draft row's 3.8 and 3.5 ms of device time, 31 percent of the embedded drafter's chain and two thirds of what the output head's product costs beside it.
- **Cause:** the kernel reduced a row in one workgroup, so 256 lanes of one compute unit walked the row's 248320 logits, which a draft row keeps in host-visible memory.
- **Fix:** a row of more than 4096 ids is reduced by a workgroup a slice into partials and then by a workgroup a row over them, in slice order by the same comparison, the row's rules (a NaN, a largest that is not finite, an invalid prior id) applied once. An argmax has no rounding, so the ids are those of one workgroup; a shorter row, and a call recorded without barriers, keep the one-workgroup form.
- **Measured, the kernel alone on a backend that timestamps** (`backend-vulkan` prints it: one row of 248320 logits, 50 calls, the kernel's bucket a row, alone and after the head's product; ms a row):

  | card | logits in | one workgroup a row, alone / after the head | in slices, alone / after the head |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | MI50, Linux | host-visible memory, where a draft row's are | 1.292 / 1.221 | 0.084 / 0.088 |
  | MI50, Linux | device memory | 0.763 / 0.528 | 0.021 / 0.024 |
  | Radeon VII, Windows | host-visible memory | 1.349 / 1.290 | 0.162 / 0.163 |
  | Radeon VII, Windows | device memory | 0.527 / 0.492 | 0.026 / 0.028 |

  The bucket is the same alone and after the head, and the wall time of a call moves with it (on the MI50 3.05 ms for the head and the argmax in one workgroup against 1.96 in slices), so the time is the kernel's own and not a wait behind the head. In a draft row's own case, host-visible logits, the kernel falls from about 1.2 to 0.09 ms on the MI50, about fifteen times.
- **Measured in generation, the gate's timing round** (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, `generate --drafter embedded`, main 0ae6d88a8 against the branch built the same way, in the order main, branch, branch, main, default clocks; tokens a second, the branch over main): one MI50 +3.85 percent on a code edit, +5.03 on free chat and +2.64 on a summary; a tensor group of two +7.88, +5.70 and +5.54; generation without drafts unchanged. One prompt a kind, so these are that round's figures and not a workload's. The kernel alone on that MI50 in the gate's run: 1.33 to 1.42 ms a row before and 0.084 to 0.097 in slices.
- **Identity, the gate's:** 44 runs of that model with the embedded drafter, greedy and seeded, on one MI50 and on the group, give main's ids and main's `drafts kept:` lines, so the drafts are the same tokens; the ISA screen shows `argmax_rows` alone differing, the row kernels' counts as they were.
- **Gates, at fc98e9984 on main 0ae6d88a8, each from its own exit status:** the builds, the first commit alone failing to compile `backend-vulkan`, CTest with `backend-vulkan` on an MI50, the suite on a device, the identity and timing above, the Radeon VII tests on Windows, the hosted run. Then stacked on perf/draft-timing 7da7bb52c, a conflict in this file alone and none in code, `src/` unchanged: the builds, CTest with `backend-vulkan` three times, `docs`, `dead-code` and the hosted run again.
- **Left for a change of its own:** a draft row's logits in device memory, which the same table puts at 0.02 ms a row against 0.08; it touches `Model::draft`, whose first member keeps them host-visible for `Model::draft_logits`.
- **A measurement of mine that was void, recorded so it is not reused:** a first timing forced the one-workgroup form by recording without barriers, which let sixteen calls overlap on the device and read as 0.06 to 0.10 ms a row on both cards; those lines measured the overlap. A per-row submission and read-back in the chain, guessed at as the cause meanwhile, does not exist: `Model::draft` records every step and submits once.
- **Tests:** `backend-vulkan`'s drafter cases, id for id against the CPU, with and without prior ids: 64 rows a call of 37 logits, of a slice less one id and plus one, and of 248320; a tie between two ids, in one slice or in two as the row's length puts them, and between the first id and the last; the largest in the first slice and in the last; an infinity in the middle and in the last slice; a NaN first and last; a row of -infinity; an invalid prior id.
## What a draft costs by phase: the chain, the verify and the output head timed apart (2026-10-12, branch perf/draft-timing, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** the cost profile of 2026-10-12 read a draft's cost off whole `generate` runs by draft count (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0: a row inside the four-column verify 4 to 7 ms, the fourth draft 12 to 20 ms more), and the output head's read for a draft row was an estimate from bytes, about 2 ms. No command timed a chain or a verify on its own, `bench --model` took no draft count, `--profile` read one device only, and the head's products were timed under the same kernel names as every other product. Two decisions wait on those figures: whether a reduced draft head is worth building, and what the fourth draft costs and where.
- **`bench --model --drafter embedded|FILE`:** after the rollback it times, for each draft count from 0 to `--draft-max` (which `bench` now takes, 3 by default), the chain of that many drafts, asked of the proposer as `generate` asks it, and the verify of the last pick and that many tokens up to its logits, each as completed work, medians over `--r` repeats after one uncounted, as `bench: draft K  chain X ms, verify Y ms` with the verify's time over a plain step. Wall time of completed work, so it reads the same way on the CPU, one device, a layer split and a tensor group. The mark is sized to the longer of the rollback's rows and `--draft-max` + 1; at the default nothing about the rollback's figures changes.
- **`--profile`:** each count's chain and verify by kernel (`profile draft chain K`, `profile verify K`) in one more round. The output head's products (`Backend::matmul_logits`, which the Vulkan backend now overrides: a backend that times its dispatches marks that call's, and any other calls `matmul` with the same arguments, as the interface's default does, so no path without `--profile` or `--timing` changes) are on lines of their own, the kernel's name with ` head` after it, in every section. It takes any list of Vulkan devices and prints each device's table, where it refused all but one device.
- **`serve --timing`:** `timing.drafting_ms` and `timing.settling_ms`, the scheduler thread's time in the chains, which it waits for, and in the verifies' retracts; the chain's time is no longer counted in `assembly_ms`.
- **Not changed:** any dispatch, kernel choice or order; `bench`'s `pp`, `tg` and rollback lines at the default; every command's output without `--timing` or `--profile`.
- **Tests:** the suite's `qwen35` and `drafters` components hold the `bench: draft` lines on the CPU (a line for each count at `--draft-max` 1, 3 and 4, and the skip with its reason past the context); `server-spec` a timed scheduler's two figures on the hybrid model with its embedded drafter, the reply its reply without drafts; `cli` the flag from the help page and the refusal of `--profile` with a device that is not a Vulkan one.
- **By hand, since no hosted runner has a Vulkan device:** `bench --model --device vulkan:0 --drafter embedded --draft-max 4 --profile` on the tiny hybrid fixture with its MTP block on a Radeon VII under Windows printed each count's chain and verify tables with the head's line in both (`matmul_row_f32_1col head`, 5 percent of a chain's device time on that fixture, which says nothing of a real model). A profile of two devices is run with the measurement this change exists for.
- **Measured with it, the figures it was built for** (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, one MI50 and a tensor group of two MI50s, default clocks, `--p 512 --n 32 --drafter embedded`, two rounds, built at this branch's 0fdffd0d2 and 8ccfc7e98, which agree; no reference-runtime row and no figure at depth, the 16384-token run having been stopped):
  - A draft row of the chain, device ms: 3.82 on one card and 3.52 on the group, of which the output head 1.82 and 1.81 (48 and 51 percent), `argmax_rows` 1.18 and 1.14, the MTP block's products and the rest 0.80 and 0.55; 4.1 and 4.0 ms of wall time. Each device of a group reads the head whole for a draft row, so a group does not shorten the chain.
  - A verify of the last pick and K drafts, wall ms, K from 0 to 7: one card 43.0, 51.2, 52.4, 53.1, 67.7, 73.1, 78.0, 83.1, then 128.9 at 8 and 161.0 at 12; the group 29.5, 33.5, 36.2, 37.6, 44.5, 47.1, 49.9, 52.6, then 80.4 at 8 and 98.7 at 12. The step at the fourth draft is the products' change from the four-column to the eight-column build, 92 percent of it on both placements, and the steps at 8 and 12 the wider builds.
  - A chain of three is 18 percent of a three-draft round on one card and 23 on the group. The rollback's own call is 0.4 to 1.0 ms and does not move with a mark of 8 rows against 4.
  - What they decided, by conditions written down before they were read: a reduced draft head is not built now (the chain is under a fifth of the round on one card; its best case is 8 to 11 percent of a round); `argmax_rows`, a third of the chain, is reduced in slices on a branch of its own; a draft of the history longer than `--draft-max` is built only with the pass price learning a pass's cost by its width.
- **Gates, at 8ccfc7e98 on main b783743a4, each read from its own exit status on the test machine:** the builds; the first commit alone failing as said; CTest; the CPU suite with its tools required; Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 the same ids and logits as main on the CPU and on one MI50; the suite on the MI50; `backend-vulkan` and `server-resume`'s device half; `--profile` printing the ` head` lines on one device and a table a device on a group of two; one timing round against main level; the linked dead-code check; on Windows the build, the CTests named above and the Radeon VII profile; the hosted run. After the rebase onto main a6f72aa75, which conflicted in one line of `docs/src/cli-main.md` and in no code, the builds, CTest and the hosted run again.

## A request arriving while a job reads its conversation takes the job's rows over (2026-10-12, branch fix/request-takes-job, lands by fast-forward)

- **Observed in production (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, a tensor group of two MI50s, a pool of 262144 KV tokens):** after a turn the server reads the conversation's next-turn ids ahead, a job, here up to 250k rows; the user's next message arrived while that job was reading, at 10:53 and 12:51 UTC on 2026-10-12, and each time the request reused nothing and read the conversation from its first token, about 38 minutes, with `reread.since_start.cancelled` rising.
- **The defect, in the round's order:** the pool being one conversation wide, the waiting request did not fit beside the job, so `run` called `yield_jobs`, which releases a job's sequence and blocks, before `enter` could look at the job as a source. The rows the job had read were discarded and read again.
- **Fix:** `Scheduler::hand_jobs`, in the round before `yield_jobs`, so only where a job would give way: a queued request at its first admission that can fork more of a job's rows than of any history kept gets them. The job's history becomes a donor with its blocks through `park`, the path a finished job already takes, and `enter` forks and consumes that donor by the rules every donor follows, so the reservation changes hands in the one ledger and admission has one owner. The job ends where the request's prompt holds all its ids, and is queued to start again from that donor otherwise.
- **Where the fork is:** `shareable`'s answer, not the job's length: on a model that keeps a state the job's last kept state, at a whole block, and nothing where the request's prompt parts from the job's ids below it; on one that does not, the whole blocks they share.
- **Unchanged where the request fits beside the job:** it forks the running job's rows and the job reads on, as before.
- **Left as it was:** a job in a pass is passed by until that pass has retired, as when it gives way; a request that fits beside a job in a pass is still admitted at once from what is kept and does not wait for the job, a wait that would need its own case at two passes in flight; and the second place a job gives way, after a request could not grow, has no handover before it.
- **What it does not hand over:** a job that kept no state of its own for want of a checkpoint slot; a job to another conversation's request, which still makes it give way and start again; a paused request resuming, which has its own history. A job's pass that fails ends the job by the path it had, before any handover.
- **Tests:** `server-resume`, the synthetic Q8_0 model and the hybrid one, the request submitted from the scheduler's thread as the job's pass reaches 528 rows: the pool full of the job, and the job in the one seat, 512 reused from one job handed over and none given way (the failing commit: 0 and 256 reused, the job giving way); a first follower leaving; sent from another thread; an edit below the job's kept state; another conversation's request; one checkpoint slot. Each reply is a fresh model's.
- **Not covered by a case, and why:** rows of another class, which a request at its first admission cannot have against a job's on the CPU test backends, both taking the class of every longer prompt (on a device whose tile split puts a short follower in another class `shareable` gives nothing and the job gives way as before); and a job's pass failing at the moment of a handover, there being no fixture that fails a job's pass alone.

## A message boundary is not a history: a conversation larger than the host tier is read back from disk (2026-10-12, branch fix/boundary-is-not-a-history, lands by fast-forward)

- **Observed in production (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, a tensor group of two MI50s, `--drafter embedded` among its flags, a pool of 262144 KV tokens, a host tier of 12.2 GiB, a disk tier with keep):** a conversation of about 255k tokens was read from its first token on most turns, about 38 minutes to the first token; one such turn began at 10:53 UTC on 2026-10-12, after the server's log had reported 18002 MiB written to disk at 09:08 UTC. The log showed message boundaries kept in host memory, the disk tier's hits and waits at 0, no promotion, and no line saying why.
- **The defect:** `Scheduler::prefetch` decided whether to read a waiting request's history from disk by comparing the path on disk with the most that memory holds, and counted a message boundary as holding it. A boundary is a state alone and serves only together with a history in memory that holds its rows. Here the conversation's copy, 17.6 GiB, is larger than the host tier, so when another conversation's small request took its blocks nothing in memory held its rows, while its boundary stayed at exactly the position the disk's path ends at: the disk was never asked, and the request was admitted with nothing.
- **Fix:** a boundary counts only where a history in memory holds its rows (`rows_held`), the rule the same function already applied to a state alone on disk.
- **No silent path any more:** a read that is not started prints the history's length and the reason and is counted (`reuse.disk.since_start.refused`); a read through host memory beyond the tier prints a line as it starts; a donor too large for the host tier that leaves the devices before its files are whole on disk prints a line and is counted in `lost_before_written`, which until now counted host entries alone.
- **What the read asks of the host in that shape:** it is read through host memory beyond the tier, taking the tier's idle slabs first and the rest fresh, and the fresh slabs must leave the host the pool's fixed reserve. A 17.6 GiB history beside a 12.2 GiB tier needs between 5.4 GiB free beyond the reserve, the whole tier standing idle, and 17.6 GiB, none of it idle; where the host does not have it the read is refused with its line and the request reads its prompt, as before this change but said.
- **Reproduced and held** (`server-resume`, the hybrid model over four CPUs, a pool of 1024 tokens, a host tier of 3 slabs, a 768-token history being 4): a turn, its job and the idle write, another conversation's request, the follow-up. The failing commit reuses 0 tokens with no history read; the fix reuses 768 through one read. Two more arms: no host memory for the read, refused and counted, nothing reused; and the other request sent before any idle moment, nothing on disk and the history counted lost.
- **Left, each put to the design review and not built:** a donor too large for the tier is still lost when taken before an idle moment wrote it, now counted and said; a request arriving while the job reads the same history makes the job give way and discards its rows; a job never reads from disk.

## The host pool keeps a fixed reserve and gives idle slabs back to a host short of memory (2026-10-11, branch fix/host-pool-pressure, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** the test machine ran out of memory and went down on 2026-10-11 with production on it. The cause is not proved and this record does not claim it; the review's reading of main found three weaknesses in how the host tier's pool meets a host short of memory, each rechecked against the code and true. Evidence read later that day points elsewhere for the fault itself, to card buffers the driver moved to system memory when another job did not fit beside production's, also unproved; this change bounds the server's own host pool and does not protect against that.
- **The three, as they were:** (1) every fresh slab was checked against a reserve of a twentieth of what the host had free at that moment (`CpuBackend::host_reserve` in `detail::host_room`), so the reserve shrank with the memory: a 64 MiB slab still passed with 67.4 MiB free. (2) Slabs a copy had released stayed in the pool whatever the host's state: `trim_host` was called only against the tier's own cap. (3) Since the idle growth landed, a tier is resident seconds after a start, so two servers' tiers, each sized from the memory free at its own start, are both taken.
- **Done, at the pool's owner (`src/model/history.hpp`):** the reserve is fixed as the model is made, a twentieth of what the host has then, as the fit's is. `Model::host_admits` is the one rule every fresh slab passes, a copy's, a read's and an idle step's, all through `alloc_host`: the slabs must leave the reserve, and growth nothing waits for must leave twice it. `Model::host_yield` gives idle slabs back to a host below the reserve, as many as cover what it is short by, and never a slab a copy holds, so paused requests' histories, donors and reads or writes in flight are untouched.
- **Done, in the scheduler:** once a second (`host_pressure`, for which an idle server now wakes while it has a host tier) it yields where the host is short, through the recorder hold, and otherwise arms the idle growth again; `grow_host` asks the pool for each copy by the slabs that copy would take anew, so a last step smaller than four is taken and a shortest copy larger than four is asked for whole. Slabs given back at the reserve are not taken again until the host has twice the reserve free, which is what keeps it from giving and taking in turn. A copy refused is not kept and a read refused is not made, each with its line, and the request reads its prompt, as before.
- **What counts the runtime's own pending allocations once:** a slab is resident as `alloc` returns, zero-filled on the device backend and value-initialized on the CPU, so the next reading of the host's memory has it; within one call the fresh slabs are admitted together before the first is taken. Nothing is subtracted from the kernel's estimate, no process is looked up and no file system is named.
- **No flag and no number to choose:** the tier's size stays a cap. The constants are the existing twentieth, twice it for optional growth, and a look a second, each with its reason beside it. `/v1/health` gains `reuse.host.now.allocated_bytes` and `reuse.host.since_start.yielded_bytes`.
- **What it is not:** a guarantee. The rule reads a figure another process can change the next moment; two servers that look at once can both pass. It bounds this server's own growth and lets it step back; it does not stop a neighbour.
- **One bounded monitored case (three servers of 15f6a6b70, Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 on one MI50 each, `--host-cache-bytes` 1 GiB each, started 20 s apart, idle, stopped 10 s apart; a sample every 2 s; `pool-15f6a6b70` on the test machine), for attribution only:** each server's pool reached 1024 MiB allocated with nothing held, and its card's GTT in use rose by 1097 MiB as it did and fell back as it stopped; Shmem did not move with any of the three (0.11 GiB before the first and after it, 0.03 GiB through the other two, the change being another agent's servers ending); MemAvailable fell from 6.04 to 4.47 GiB between the two samples around the first server's start, about 1.6 GiB, model and pool together. So on this driver the pool's slabs are counted in the card's GTT figure and in the kernel's estimate of available memory, and not as shared memory. The case started at 8.26 GiB available and stood at 6.0 GiB when the first server came up, another agent's work having taken the difference; the second server's pool stood at 256 MiB for one sample at 5.4 GiB available and reached its cap once memory rose to 23.6 GiB. No slab was yielded and the case did not press the host.
- **Tests:** `kv-cache` and `server-resume`, the host's free memory given by the test (`ModelOptions::host_memory`): the reserve at its edge after memory has fallen, optional growth at twice it, the yield of idle slabs alone, a held copy's bytes and restore; through the scheduler the growth stopping at ten slabs of twelve, its last step the two that are left, one slab given back and none taken again across three looks, the held histories serving, a read refused whole, and over six CPUs a shortest copy of six slabs refused with twelve free and taken with fourteen, which fails where the copy is not asked for by its own size (the failing commit: `kv-cache` fails with "a copy that leaves the host less than the reserve fixed as the model was made", the copy being taken, and `server-resume` in its pool case, the idle growth there running to the tier's cap: with "the idle growth standing at the ten slabs the host has room for within a minute" where the count is never seen at ten, or with "the scheduler looking at the host's memory within a minute" where it is, the scheduler then making no further round; both were seen).
- **Left:** the default tier's size, half of what the host has free at a start, is unchanged, the review having no measurement for another fraction; the look is once a second, so idle slabs outstay pressure by that long; the logits rows and staging a server takes at its start are outside the pool and outside this rule.

## An idle server takes the host tier's slabs ahead (2026-10-11, branch perf/host-slab-growth, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** a fresh slab of host memory is zero-filled as it is taken, and a history read back from disk took all of its slabs at once, in `start_read` on the scheduler's thread and under its lock, before the read started: 2.0 s for the 5.2 GiB of a 76k-token conversation's first turn after a restart (the read profile of 2026-10-08, below), during which no pass is formed and no request is admitted.
- **Done:** `Scheduler::grow_host`. While nothing is active, waiting or to be read again, the loop takes the tier's slabs, four fresh ones a round, or the shortest copy's where that copy needs more, with no sleep between: it allocates copies of histories within the tier's free room and releases them at once, which leaves their slabs idle in the model's pool, where a later copy or read finds them. The four are counted where the pool is, a device at a time (`Model::host_fresh`), since idle slabs on one device do not serve another, and the step's history is chosen by `grow_tokens` in the policy core; a model whose shortest copy needs more than four grows by that copy alone. No backend or store code changes, and no result's bits; `src/model/history.hpp` gains the count, so the numerics fingerprint moves.
- **What it costs:** the tier's memory is the server's from seconds after its start, where on main it was taken as copies needed it and then kept; `--host-cache-bytes` in USAGE says so. The default tier is up to half of what the host has free, so a server that never evicts a conversation now holds that much, page cache and neighbours on a shared host paying for it; no new flag, the size given or defaulted being the bound. A request that arrives while a step runs waits for that step; how long a step takes was not measured.
- **Measured (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, a tensor group of two MI50s, the embedded drafter, production's flags with a scratch cache directory, llmx on its two cards and four cores, default clocks; main 704f1b7b6 and the branch built the same way from detached trees): a turn of 76018 prompt tokens kept at a stop, 76 files and 5.5 GB, then its next turn, 76078 tokens of which 76032 are read back, sent 10 s after a restart's disk tier is ready; three starts an arm, interleaved, each from a copy of the kept directory. At the head that lands:**

  | | main 704f1b7b6 | the branch |
  |---|---|---|
  | the longest answer of `/v1/health` during the turn, asked every 10 ms | 2223, 2058, 3063 ms | 100, 632, 4 ms |
  | first token after | 8.11, 7.92, 9.10 s | 5.94, 6.45, 5.83 s |
  | waited for the read, as the server counts it | 4432, 4437, 4628 ms | 4384, 4382, 4405 ms |
  | host tier's limit at that start | 9.8, 4.0, 8.8 GB | 5.4, 4.0, 11.4 GB |

  And with the turn sent as the tier becomes ready, one start an arm: first token after 7.73 and 6.03 s, the longest health answer 1967 and 205 ms.
- **The same shape an hour earlier, at the head before the step's bound was counted a device (ca557acac), kept as measured:** the longest health answer 2616, 2172, 2059 ms on main and 9, 80, 26 ms on the branch; first token after 9.04, 10.45, 9.20 s and 8.48, 8.53, 10.53 s; the read waited for 4911, 6831, 5655 ms and 6853, 6591, 8892 ms.
- **The same shape once more under a monitor, at f9343ed75, f81dbc57b's code with its comments reworded (every 5 s the load, the processor's counters, the eight busiest processes, the disks' sector counters and the cards' busy share, the same for both arms, in `slabmon-f9343ed75/monitor.txt` on the test machine).** The process column is `ps`'s share of a process's whole life and not of the interval, so flag 1 says a busy process existed and not that it ran during a start; what processes did during each start was not observed. Flags declared before the run: (1) a process not the start's own server above a core, (2) the processors busy above half in all, (3) the disks reading more than 1 GB beyond the turn's 5.5 GB, (4) the start's cards busy before the turn. The machine was busy throughout, load 10 to 15, other agents' builds and a benchmark of another runtime among the processes; five of the six starts are flagged, and all are kept:

  | start | first token after | the longest health answer | waited for the read | host tier's limit | flags |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | main 1 | 36.58 s | 4022 ms | 30869 ms | 2.0 GB | 1, 3 (37.0 GB read by the disks) |
  | the branch 1 | 10.51 s | 20 ms | 8942 ms | 6.5 GB | 1, 3 (28.2 GB) |
  | main 2 | 8.58 s | 2747 ms | 4338 ms | 7.5 GB | none |
  | the branch 2 | 6.04 s | 174 ms | 4411 ms | 5.3 GB | 3 (25.4 GB) |
  | main 3 | 11.94 s | 3769 ms | 6678 ms | 6.0 GB | 1, 3 (27.9 GB) |
  | the branch 3 | 11.99 s | 13 ms | 10350 ms | 7.4 GB | 3 (22.8 GB) |

  Under that load the read and with it the first token moved by seconds from start to start in both arms, the first start of main with a tier of 2.0 GB reading through memory beyond it for 31 s; the longest health answer was 2.7 to 4.0 s on main and 0.2 s at most on the branch in every start, flagged or not.
- **What the figures say and do not:** `/v1/health` takes the scheduler's lock, so its longest answer is a measure of how long the server answered nothing, the handler's and the connection's time included; it is not a timer on the lock. That latency fell from 2.1 to 4.0 s to 0.6 s at most in every start of the three blocks, eighteen starts. The turn's own first token came 2.1 s sooner in the second block, where the read's wait varied least, 4.4 to 4.6 s, and was within the read's variation in the other two; the claim is the stall, and the first token only as far as that one block shows it. The default tier's limit, half of what the host had free, differed from start to start and crossed the copy's 5.5 GB, so some starts kept a host entry and some read through memory beyond the tier; every start is kept. No monitor of the machine's activity ran beside the first two blocks, which is a fault of the measurement and not a property of the machine; the third ran under one and shows the machine busy, so none of the three is shown to be uncontended. On main the server's wait is counted from after the allocation, so the wait rows are not the whole span.
- **What it does not reach, and why not another way:** a server that is never idle grows on demand as before, and a copy read through host memory beyond the tier still takes its slabs at the read. Filling slabs on another thread is closed twice: a device takes calls from its stage's thread alone, and the pages' first touch on the copying thread cost 9.7 s for 5.2 GiB where the fill costs 1.0 s (the unfilled allocation, measured and rejected on 2026-10-08).
- **Left, not built here:** the store reads its files on one thread, 4 MiB a chunk, about 1.8 GB/s where the pool gives 3.0 GB/s to four streams of 16 MiB (a read-only probe of 2026-10-11), and checksums and copies each chunk after reading it, 0.7 and 0.8 s of the long read; parallel reads and the checksum beside the read are the next two levers on the first token.
- **Tests:** `server-resume`: a scheduler over two CPUs with a host tier of six slabs and nothing to do must take six host-visible allocations and no more, and four turns that evict and promote must allocate none (the failing commit: none taken within the minute the case waits). `server-passes`: the step's rule by hand, four slabs idle on one device and none on the other. `kv-cache`: the fresh count beside a copy holding the pool and with the pool idle.
- **Gates, at the code of this record's commit, each read from its own exit status on the test machine:** a CPU build (0, no warning), CTest (0, 42 of 42), the CPU suite with its tools required (0), Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 the same ids and logits as main 704f1b7b6 on the CPU and on one MI50 (`cmp` 0 each), the suite on the MI50 (0), with the components that need a tool beside the binary run again there once every target was built (0: `decode-probe`, `drafters`, `mxfp4` and `qwen35` on the card, `device-reference`, `split` and `tensor-split` on the CPU paths they name themselves), `server-resume`'s device half on the MI50 (0, 11575 checks); the two Qwen3.5 real-model baselines skipped in the full suites for want of their fixture files; the measurement blocks above as the timing round; on Windows CTest 43 of 43 by its status; the hosted run.
- **Reviewed:** by XDEV, the gating reviewer: one finding, a step not held to four fresh slabs where the idle slabs stand on another device, taken and fixed at the pool's owner, and the health row's wording. The plan was read by F2DEV on 2026-10-08, who set the whole cap as the bound.

## A job shares every id a history holds (2026-10-11, branch fix/job-shares-its-ids, lands by fast-forward)

- **The defect, on main since jobs:** `Scheduler::shareable` shared at most a history less its last token, the token a request's pass computes for its logits. A job asks for no logits, yet the rule held for it too, so a job whose ids a donor held whole could share one block less than the donor held; on a model that keeps a state, where a donor is forked at its checkpoint or not at all, that was nothing, and the job read the whole history.
- **Where it showed:** after a restart, where the history read from disk for a turn is the one the turn's job is then given, written by the job before. Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, a tensor group of two MI50s, the embedded drafter, production's flags, a 30749-token chat's first turn after a restart, five starts of five: the turn's first token after 3.45 to 3.53 s, and the job behind it 98.1 to 99.2 s, reading 30784 rows. Without a restart the job forks the donor of the job before, which ends lower, so it stayed hidden; the proved adoption met the same want and hid it with the entry at its fork.
- **What a request arriving meanwhile saw:** the next turn sent 5 s after the reply gave its first token after 2.47 s against 0.57 s once the job has ended; it did not wait behind the job and the job was not cancelled.
- **Fix:** a job shares up to all of its ids, on every model: on one without a state a job whose ids end on a whole block forks that last block where it read it again. A job that forked every id from a donor still standing completes without parking: it leaves no second donor of the same tokens, takes no checkpoint slot and writes nothing, and the donor it forked keeps the boundary, supersedes what the job's donor would and is itself no longer superseded, being the conversation's newest holder (`complete_jobs`). Where admission consumed the donor it forked, the job parks as before and is the one holder.
- **Test:** `server-resume`, on the synthetic Q8_0 model and the hybrid one, under a disk tier with keep: the ids a turn's next turn begins with given once and given twice; the second job must read no row (the failing commit: 128 rows of 512 on the first model, 256 on the second, which forks only at a checkpoint) and leave the donors, the checkpoint slots, the reserved blocks and the files the stopped server keeps as one job left them; given again after a job of a block more, whose donor superseded the first's, they are forked whole from that donor. The ids given twice stand in for a donor read back from disk; the restart itself is held by the run on the cards below, not by a case.
- **After, the same shape and the same kept chat, three starts at the code of this record's commit:** the turn's first token after 3.52 to 3.88 s as before, the reply read again after 1.0 s and 64 rows in two starts, against 98.1 to 99.2 s and 30784 rows; with the next turn arriving 5 s after the reply, that turn's first token after 0.60 s against 2.47 s, and both jobs ended 5.8 s after the reply.
- **Can the donor that stands for the job be one an earlier job superseded:** yes, where the ids are given, then longer ids, then the first again, the longer job's donor having superseded the first's; the arm clears the mark on the donor it keeps, the conversation's newest holder. The case runs that order and holds that the third job reads nothing; no assertion sees the mark itself, the state at the ids being kept by its boundary either way.

## Another build's entries adopted and proved (2026-10-10, branch feat/disk-adopt-proved, lands by fast-forward)

- **Why:** the disk tier adopts only entries of its own numerics fingerprint, so an upgrade starts with an empty cache although most upgrades change no bit of a history. Production holds 283 files, 21 GB, of conversations whose requests average 107k prompt tokens, each read again in full by the first server of a new build.
- **Done:** `serve --disk-cache-adopt exact|proved`, `exact` the default and what main did. Under `proved` a server takes the entries of another build of the same model, layout and entry version unproved, and the first request of each conversation proves its own path ([DISK-TIER](DISK-TIER.md), Adopting another build's entries): its own first block compared with the file's, its cache restored at the highest point below the path's end where a history can be forked, the rows from there to the end computed, and those rows, as far back as the path's last file holds them, and the state at the end compared, byte for byte. Equal, the files are this build's, their headers rewritten; unequal, they and every other unproved file of that build are deleted and the request computes its history from the start.
- **Who decides:** the tier. `DiskTier::plan`, `prove`, `proving`, `compare` and `abandon` hold which positions are compared, the comparison, the claim and the deletion; the scheduler computes the rows, copies a block and hands it over (`Scheduler::prove`, `unprove`, two slice stops and the plan in `prefetch`, 140 lines). Unproved files are no part of this build's index: a path, a missing range and a state are found among its own files alone, so nothing reads, forks, renews or rewrites one, and the proof's read is the tier's own, restored into the proving request's sequence and into no shared pool until the proof has ended equal.
- **What a proof does not prove:** the rows between the first block and the last stretch, a row class neither holds, a depth or width they did not reach; and the last stretch is computed over the files' own rows below it, so a build that differs only in the rows between passes. `exact` stays the default for that reason, and USAGE and OPERATING say it beside the flag.
- **The store:** an adopted entry keeps its header and a file beside it keeps the identity it was written under; a claim rewrites the identity and the header's checksum in place and has them reach the disk before that file goes. A start settles a claim cut short by the checksum on disk, between the kept identity and the directory's, the claimant's, and then applies its own policy, so a third build never has an entry as proved because a second proved it. A step that fails, the kept identity not written, a header not put right, a claim's sync, keeps the entry for a later start instead of deleting it.
- **Measured, production's shape (Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0, a tensor group of two MI50s, the embedded drafter, a scratch cache directory, llmx alone on its two cards and four cores, default clocks), a chat of 29146 tokens grown over three turns and kept at a stop by a build of the same bits under another fingerprint, then its fourth turn, 29465 prompt tokens, after a restart:**

  | the server that takes the fourth turn | tokens reused | prompt ms | first token after | the reply read again after |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | the build that wrote the entries | 29312 | 1567, 1496 | 4.81, 3.98 s | 1.0 s |
  | another build, `--disk-cache-adopt proved` | 29248 | 2329, 2334, 2394, 2295 | 5.55, 5.47, 5.39, 5.46 s | 1.0 s |
  | another build, by default (`exact`) | 0 | 93772 | 93.88 s | not measured |

  The four servers gave the same reply. The first and third rows are one start each with one and two turns; the second is four starts. A proof cost 0.6 to 1.6 s over a plain read from disk, the first block and the last 64 tokens computed and 2.0 GiB restored once, against 93.9 s for the prompt; 31 of the conversation's 32 files were claimed, the one left an earlier state no path ends at. The cost per conversation is its first block and its last turn's rows, whatever its length, so production's 100k-token conversations pay the same two stretches.
- **What comparing the whole stretch costs, the same shape with a third turn whose reply is 1400 tokens, so the fourth turn's proof computes 1472 rows and compares 1024 of them, 16 blocks, where the head before compared the last 64:**

  | the server that takes the fourth turn, 30749 prompt tokens | tokens reused | prompt ms | first token after |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | another build, `proved`, the last block compared (7ee63fbde) | 29248 | 6953, 6959 | 10.14, 9.98 s |
  | another build, `proved`, the stretch compared | 29248 | 6992, 6884 | 10.08, 9.95 s |
  | the build that wrote the entries, one start | 30720 | 786 | 3.91 s |

  Nothing measurable: the rows are computed either way and the file is in memory, so the wider comparison is a copy of fifteen more blocks. The proof here costs 6 s over a plain read, which is the last turn's 1472 rows read again; 32 of 32 files claimed and the same reply from all five.
- **A defect the measurement found, fixed before review:** after a proved turn the job that reads the reply again read the whole history, 94.1 s of device time behind the reply, since the tier's copy of the path was released and nothing it could fork was left where a read from disk leaves a host entry. A proof that ends equal now leaves its copy a host entry; the job then takes 1.0 s, as after a read by the same build, and a case holds it.
- **A third, found by the device cases:** on a device a reply's rows are another kind than a prompt's, so the next turn's path ends inside the kept file; the proof holds for the path, the request reuses it, and the file, used in part, is not claimed and stays unproved until its age takes it. The case had expected the whole file.
- **A fourth, found by tracing a server of one checkpoint slot at the review's word:** the restore took the slot, the slice at the path's end found none for its state, and the proof was given up after its rows were computed, more work than no proof. Such a server now starts none on a model that keeps a state.
- **A second, found by reading:** a slice that reached a message boundary at the path's end kept its state in host memory before the comparison there. The state is now kept only once the proof has ended equal.
- **Tests:** `disk-store`: the adoption and claim cases, the matrix of five header states by three builds starting next, and three failing steps, each keeping the entry. `server-resume`: the proof on the synthetic Q8_0 model and on the hybrid one, with the job and the turn after it; a byte planted in the first block, the last block and the state under checksums that hold; a client leaving between the comparisons from the scheduler's thread; a one-turn hybrid conversation left unproved and replaced; and the dense case with its fault on a device where one opens. `cli`: the flag's values.
- **Traced at the review's word:** `park` takes the scheduler's lock itself further down, so no caller holds it where `unprove` takes it; the request's reservation, made at admission for its whole history, stands across the reset and the restore, which gives blocks back and takes fewer on the scheduler's thread with nothing between; one checkpoint slot, above; the device cases ran on an MI50 and found the third defect.
- **Reviewed:** XDEV the store at b9f96ce98, four findings, all taken; O5REV the design twice and the change at 7ee63fbde, five points and two smaller ones, all taken, and the head that lands.
- **What it does not reach:** a conversation of one turn on a model that keeps a state has no state below its end and is read again, and so is every conversation on such a model served with one checkpoint slot; an earlier state of a proved conversation that no path ends at, and a file a path uses in part, stay unproved until their age takes them; `proved` without `--disk-cache-keep` is refused.
## An idle server's writes start once its idle moment has passed (2026-10-10, branch fix/idle-write-start, lands by fast-forward)

- **The defect, on main since the idle writes:** `Scheduler::run` took the idle moment as its wait's bound only while it lay ahead (`next_disk_bound`), and told `disk_round` a round was idle only if the round began at or after it. A wake shortly before the moment, the store becoming ready or a write ending, gave a round that was not idle, and by the next wait the moment was past, so the wait had no bound and no idle round ran until something else woke the loop: within a minute where files and an age limit gave the age check, and not before the next request or the stop's flush where the disk was still empty. No wrong byte and no loss at a clean stop; a crash in that window lost the turn.
- **Found:** in a new case of the kept-conversations work that used an idle time of 50 ms, where it struck in three of about twelve runs on Windows; O5REV confirmed it against the code.
- **Fix:** the moment bounds the wait until a round has run idle since it was set (`idled_`), whether it lies ahead or behind; after that round it bounds nothing, so a past moment cannot make the loop spin.
- **Test:** `server-resume`, with an idle time of nothing, so the moment is past as it is set and the fault is certain and not a race: a turn's entry must be written with nothing else to wake the loop (the failing commit: never within the minute the case waits), and the timed scheduler must then run fewer than a hundred rounds in a fifth of a second, which a bound that kept holding fails with 268751.
- **Gates, at the code of this record's commit:** on the test machine a CPU build without warnings, CTest 42 of 42, the CPU suite, and Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 the same ids and logits as main b9debf760 on the CPU; on Windows CTest 43 of 43 and the suite's `docs` and `dead-code`; the hosted run.
- **Reviewed:** by O5REV, the gating reader; found by the kept-conversations developer.

  reported with the selected fast path or fallback. llmx's runtime knobs stay
  flags; temporary development variables do not ship as hidden controls.
  ROCm is an off-by-default build option beside Vulkan, with an independently
  optional RCCL build option under it; both config forms stay in sync.
- **Probe checkpoint:** a standalone 500-dependent-add launch smoke passes
  under HIP eager submission, HIP graph replay and the existing Vulkan backend
  on one MI50: each checks 64 outputs equal to 500 in all 25 chains, 4,800
  checked values in total. It uses PCI 0000:89:00.0 on root pci0000:80, separate
  from production's pci0000:c0, with bounded processes and no peer barriers.
  The community image is pinned to SHA256
  `1e1a116b443f2b474e7fe14933552013ef68003364d7ec194d6101efa92faa87`,
  HIP 7.2.53211 and clang 22. Both probe sources build with warnings as errors.
  Concurrent correctness tests make its recorded timings diagnostic only;
  this proves neither a speed gain nor peer visibility. Source, hashes and
  outputs are in `/zpool1/llmx-xdev-validation/rocm-probe-20261009`.
  The same standalone source also compiles for gfx1151 with warnings as errors;
  that is compile coverage of this launch probe only, with no Strix Halo run
  or backend-support claim.
- **Peer probe build:** the standalone peer-memory check compiles independently
  for gfx906 and gfx1151 with `-O3 -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror` in the
  same pinned image, without access to any GPU. It tests public ordinary,
  fine-grained and uncached allocations, rotating delayed submissions, guarded
  peer writes and fixed-order F32 sums after host synchronization. Source and
  binary hashes and both compile logs are in that probe directory's
  `build-peer-1`. Compilation alone qualifies no peer-memory run, device-side
  visibility protocol, collective or RCCL; the hardware checks below are separate.
- **RCCL inventory:** that image has installed `rccl` and `rccl-dev` packages
  `2.27.7.70201-81~24.04`. Their header and library live under `/usr/local`,
  outside the `/opt/rocm` prefix. The header identifies 2.27.7, the loader
  resolves the library and its dependencies, and `ncclGetVersion` returns
  success with 22707 without any GPU exposed to the container. Header/library
  hashes and all inventory attempts are retained in `rccl-inventory*.log` in
  the probe directory. This establishes availability for the planned probe,
  not MI50 communicator, graph or numerical qualification.
  `roc-obj-ls` could not inspect the library's embedded targets because the
  image lacks Perl's `File::Which`; `rccl-targets.log` retains that tooling
  failure, from which no target-support conclusion is drawn.
- **Peer hardware checkpoint:** groups of two, three and four MI50s pass all three
  public allocation modes, with the frozen source/binary and no environment
  override. Each cell runs 1, 127 and 5,120 values through 16 epochs apiece.

  | Members | Rig GPUs (PCI suffixes) | Ordinary | Fine-grained | Uncached |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 2 | 2/3 (83:00.0, 86:00.0) | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs |
  | 3 | 2/3/5 (83:00.0, 86:00.0, 8c:00.0) | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs |
  | 4 | 2/3/4/5 (83:00.0, 86:00.0, 89:00.0, 8c:00.0) | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs | 48/48 epochs |

  All directed peer links are available. Every peer payload, guard and local

  three- and four-member sums and rotating delayed submissions. All 432 epochs pass.
  `HSA_FORCE_FINE_GRAIN_PCIE` is unset; host stream synchronization separates
  writes and sums. This does not establish device-side signal visibility,
  barriers, graph replay, RCCL collectives or performance. All processes drain

  retain the checks under the probe directory. Width four ran after the peer

  gfx1151 with warnings as errors; linking it says nothing about the library's

  Each cell completes all 48 epochs at 1, 127 and 5,120 values, using the same

  The native three- and four-member cells return 3, the declared numerical
  failure, after completing every planned epoch. For the one-value positive
  cancellation case, member order gives 0 and 3 respectively; RCCL gives 1
  and 4. Different addition order explains why F32 alone cannot promise this
  contract; this is not a claim that every RCCL result is less accurate.
  Guard and transfer checks pass. Every size's communicator set initializes
  and destroys normally; all six containers drain and each card's VRAM returns
  to its measured starting value. The raw `rccl-*-*-1` records and independent
  `rccl-summary.json` retain successes and failures. No tolerance or wire
  precision was changed. Native sums at three and four members in this setup
  are ineligible for the current ordered-sum contract; the transfer path stays
  a candidate. Two-member success is scoped to these inputs. Graph replay,
  failure recovery, arbitrary bit-pattern transfers, size crossovers and
  matched performance remain unqualified, as does backend adoption.
- **Device-signal checkpoint:** the independently written one-block probe uses
  uncached system-release/acquire epoch flags, an explicit system fence from
  every peer writer, original local contributions and a consumed barrier before
  staging reuse. Shapes 1, 127, 5,120 and 5,121 run 32 changing epochs inside
  each kernel and four launches per shape over the same buffers, with rotating
  2 ms rank launch delays. No host wait separates the in-kernel phases.

  | Members | Uncached payload | Fine-grained payload | Ordinary payload |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 2 | 512/512 exact epochs | Stale payload, exit 1 | Stale payload, exit 1 |
  | 3 | 512/512 exact epochs | Stale payload, exit 1 | Stale payload, exit 1 |
  | 4 | 512/512 exact epochs | Stale payload, exit 1 | Stale payload, exit 1 |

  Each passing epoch checks every consumed contribution independently, every
  ordered F32 result, unchanged inputs, guards and the untouched self slot.
  All 1,536 uncached epochs pass with `HSA_FORCE_FINE_GRAIN_PCIE` unset.
  Every failed cell completes its first 32 signal handshakes but reads the old
  `0xa5a5a5a5` canary instead of 1.0 at the first checked remote contribution;
  it stops at that mismatch, so none of its epochs is counted as validated.
  The six failures remain in the evidence. They show why the earlier
  host-synchronized pass does not establish in-kernel payload visibility.
  Ordinary allocation is only a diagnostic control, even had it passed.
  Missing-member controls at widths two and four omit the final member's
  launch: every launched member exits at its bounded ready-epoch-1 wait,
  completing no epoch. The controls also check untouched outputs and guards.
  Polling is bounded by both 2^24 loads and 500 million shader-clock ticks;
  these are not wall-clock guarantees. The process has a 120-second timeout
  and a ten-second kill bound. This is a specific timeout check, not general
  failed-device recovery. Every process drains, its container disappears and
  all cards return to their exact pre-run VRAM use, without resets.
  Both targets compile with warnings as errors. Source SHA256 is
  `2ece4f597acfa15edc0922eb8af191aa33a1bb63e08b3b94cd9d089cfd68a8fc`,
  gfx906 binary `ed6bd8cc5c6a1e9a1126e612871cd67dc8a33a584ab96a34bfb73ed91fe4680f`.
  Emitted assembly records 104 SGPRs, 39 VGPRs and 72 scratch bytes on gfx906;
  gfx1151 records 62, 33 and 72 respectively, with no hardware claim.
  Despite the source non-temporal hint, gfx906 payload loads are ordinary
  global loads. No cause beyond the measured allocation-mode difference is
  established, and this diagnostic kernel is not performance-ready.
  The first assembly command failed because the hipcc wrapper added an unused
  link flag under warnings-as-errors; direct clang generated both assemblies
  from the unchanged source. Both attempts are retained. Raw `signal-*-1`
  records, `build-signal-2`, the frozen `signal-protocol.md` and the independently
  checked `signal-summary.json` are under the same probe evidence directory.
  Uncached staging is the next candidate; graph replay, multiple blocks,
  message-size crossovers, model execution and matched latency remain open.
- **Multi-block graph checkpoint:** a separate standalone probe uses uncached
  payloads and signals, per-block ready/consumed epochs and an ordered chain
  of 32 separate collective kernels. The same kernel runs through eager
  submission and captured graph replay. A stable device descriptor changes
  the base sequence between four launches while every payload changes.
  Each block owns the same indices on all members, including empty blocks,
  and waits only for that block on peers. Grids 1, 2, 4 and 16 are below the
  queried theoretical residency limit; shapes are 1, 127, 5,120, 5,121 and
  65,537 values. A rotating member launch is delayed 2 ms per batch.

  gfx906 binary `09eeb6bfbab2872a3937a7568a2f89ff7f427fe3b52dfc540c4191edd12d5133`.

## Vulkan int8 twin cache row width (2026-10-09, branch fix/vulkan-int8-twin-width, lands by fast-forward)

- **Goal:** reusing one activation buffer with a different matrix row width must
  give the same output as freshly packing that input for the new width.
- **Done:** the public-call regression on main `a1b8211b4` fails on an MI50:
  `int8 twin reused across matrix widths changes output`. It witnesses the
  int8 tile; 1,239,200 existing int8 outputs pass before the new case.
  The unfixed cache accepted any block-major width for a nonzero tile width,
  although addressing depends on it. The build and failed run are retained in
  `/zpool1/llmx-xdev-validation/quantizer-push-20261009/twin-width`.
  The cache owner now requires a matching block-major width while preserving
  reuse of column-major and 16-bit copies. The same MI50 test passes with
  5,120 new output values exact, alongside the existing backend checks.
  Both touched files' comments are swept: 55 blocks shortened with all
  non-comment tokens retained, and the detailed decode/count notes moved to
  the Vulkan source page. Integration with the comment checker removes
  those two files' obsolete allowances and adds no exception.
  A fresh MSVC Vulkan build after that sweep passes
  `backend-vulkan` on the Radeon VII; the int8-specific case reports zero
  there because its profile does not select int8. The compile log records
  both edited files rebuilt. Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 full-vocabulary logits agree byte
  for byte against the unchanged main runtime on CPU and Radeon VII, under
  both auto and int8 fallback (four comparisons). These quick comparisons
  cover one prompt, not the complete model or performance gates.
  Docs and dead-code checks pass; the docs check's initial misreading of a
  mathematical expression as a C++ call was corrected in prose.
  The complete fresh Windows build passes all 48 native tests in 564.37
  seconds, including the five Vulkan checks; logs are `build-all.log` and
  `ctest.log` in the branch worktree. Existing test-source shadowing and
  `sscanf` warnings remain; no warning-free build is claimed.
  A clean detached Linux build at f3dce7978 passes all 47 native tests on
  an MI50 in 594.09 seconds. All six required GGUF fixtures match their
  pinned sizes and SHA256 values; the full device suite with required tools
  and baseline passes all 28 components, including the HF, int8, MXFP4,
  qwen35, split, server and follow-up checks. These results are in
  `/zpool1/llmx-xdev-validation/int8-twin-gate-20261009/evidence`.
  All 72 model identity comparisons against the unchanged main runtime
  pass: six pinned Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 files, CPU and MI50, auto and int8,
  each with full-vocabulary prompt logits, eight fixed continuation tokens'
  full-vocabulary logits, and up to 32 generated token IDs and their text.
  The original generation comparator included timing lines and looked for
  IDs on stderr, so its 24 failure verdicts are invalid. Its raw captures
  are retained; `identity-verified.json` compares the actual IDs and text
  on stdout and records the added continuation checks. This preserves the
  existing arithmetic on these workloads; it is not a new depth gate.
  The matched timing round runs both clean builds on one MI50 (GPU4,
  PCI 0000:89:00.0), default clocks, two host threads pinned to logical
  CPUs 0 and 1 with their siblings reserved. Each model/dtype runs
  main/fixed/fixed/main, pp512/tg128, three repetitions per command,
  ubatch512 and F16 K/V. All 48 calls are retained; the table gives the mean
  of each arm's two calls in tok/s. This repair's comparison is against
  main; the phase-level mx gaps remain open and mx was not remeasured here.

- Goal: Polish the dashboard title, visualize own-history acceptance, and show per-request live rates from runtime counters.
- Done: Title is `llmx monitor`; own-history kept/not-kept totals use a compact labeled bar. Live-request cards put runtime phase, elapsed time and PP/TG rates first, with token counters collapsed per request. The throughput charts and lower secondary panels have a tighter hierarchy; range changes follow the primary throughput and request views. Thirteen focused browser assertions pass, including redraw interaction preservation. Parent's synthetic full-page Chromium review passed at 1440px desktop and 390px mobile with no horizontal overflow. Evidence is in ignored `build-dashboard-review/cdp-review.json` and `cdp-{desktop,mobile}-{top,requests,lower}.png`; source SHA256 `0c3d2bdbc80e4405f782aae550bfbfd398dd11bda223dd2dc0ee81a342a08689`.
- Deployment: The static UI landed separately by fast-forward, without changing the collector or inference runtime. The later runtime deployment `3b2a701b` added `requests.live`, enabling per-request cards after two distinct samples for a request. Servers without that API still show the unavailable state.
- Gotchas: Own-history provides lifetime drafted and kept totals only; its bar does not imply position, time-series or per-request data. Live rates are unavailable for first samples, resets and older APIs; requests can start and finish between polls without appearing, and the endpoint may omit rows above its cap. Replacing the Python collector requires browser-local polling/history (per-tab and lost on reload) or a native shared collector; serving only the static page is insufficient.
